issues.legal_issue: An unequivocal unilateral declaration of an intention to separate severs a member’s status in a Mitakshara joint Hindu family when the intention is made known to the other affected members.
material_facts: The family had continued as a joint Hindu family, and the plaintiff was its karta.
The plaintiff issued notices stating unequivocally that he intended to separate from the family.
Although the notices were intercepted before delivery, the evidence established that the other members had knowledge of their contents and of the plaintiff’s intention.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff’s status in the joint family was severed because his unequivocal intention to separate had been made known to the other members; formal dispatch to or receipt by them was not essential.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, a coparcener’s unequivocal declaration of an intention to hold his share separately effects severance of status once that intention is made known to the members from whom he seeks to separate. Communication need not take the form of formal dispatch or receipt; it must reach the affected members by a process appropriate to the circumstances. The Court relied on Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain, Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Syed Kasam v. Jorawar Singh, and Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma.

predicates.joint_family_severance_dispute: The case concerns whether a member of a joint Hindu family became separate in status.
predicates.unequivocal_intention_to_separate: A family member clearly and unambiguously declared an intention to separate and hold a share separately.
predicates.intention_made_known_to_affected_members: The declared intention reached the family members affected by it through a process appropriate to the circumstances.

issues.definition: When a joint-family severance dispute involves an unequivocal intention to separate that is made known to the affected members, the member’s joint status is severed.

issues.legal_issue: Once a communicated unilateral declaration has severed joint status, withdrawing the declaration alone does not restore the former joint status or amount to an agreement to reunite.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s unequivocal intention to separate had been communicated to the other family members and had already severed his joint status.
The plaintiff later instructed the postal authorities not to forward the notices.
There was no allegation or evidence that the family members subsequently agreed to reunite.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal did not undo the severance or restore the former joint status; reunion required a subsequent agreement, which was not proved.
issues.legal_principle: After an unequivocal intention to separate has been communicated and severance has taken effect, the declarant cannot restore the former joint status merely by revoking that intention. The members may reunite by a subsequent agreement, but the agreement must be proved as a fact. The Court approved Kurapati Radhakrishna v. Kurapati Satyanarayana.

rule.if: joint_family_severance_dispute and communicated_declaration_already_severed_status and declaration_later_withdrawn and no_subsequent_reunion_agreement

predicates.joint_family_severance_dispute: The case concerns whether a member of a joint Hindu family became separate in status.
predicates.communicated_declaration_already_severed: An unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate had reached the affected family members and severed joint status.
predicates.declaration_later_withdrawn: The declarant later attempted to withdraw the declaration of an intention to separate.
predicates.no_subsequent_reunion_agreement: The family members did not subsequently agree to reunite.

issues.definition: Where a communicated declaration has already severed joint status, withdrawing it without a subsequent reunion agreement does not restore joint status.

issues.legal_issue: Legal representatives may obtain a partition decree on a deceased plaintiff’s suit when the plaintiff consciously executed the plaint and it was filed before his death, and his separate status entitled him to seek partition.
material_facts: The plaint was prepared by an advocate who explained its contents to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff was conscious and in possession of his mental faculties when he affixed his thumb impression to the plaint and vakalatnama.
The plaint and vakalatnama were filed in court before the plaintiff died that day.
The plaintiff’s status had been severed from the joint family, and his daughters were his legal representatives.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff validly executed the plaint while conscious and understanding its contents; the suit was validly instituted, and his legal representatives were entitled to the partition decree.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the evidence established that the plaintiff understood and executed the plaint while conscious and that it was filed before his death. It relied on the evidence of the witnesses, the advocate’s countersignature on the plaint and vakalatnama, and the trial court’s assessment of the evidence. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this issue.

rule.if: partition_suit and plaintiff_consciously_understood_and_executed_plaint and plaint_filed_before_plaintiff_died and deceased_plaintiff_had_separate_status

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition of family property.
predicates.plaintiff_consciously_understood_and_exe: The plaintiff was conscious, understood the plaint’s contents, and executed it.
predicates.plaint_filed_before_plaintiff_died: The plaint was filed in court before the plaintiff died.
predicates.deceased_plaintiff_had_separate_status: The deceased plaintiff had separated in status from the joint family and was entitled to seek partition.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, where the plaintiff consciously executes and files the plaint before death and had separate status, the plaintiff’s legal representatives are entitled to the partition decree.
